source_edition: Joseph A. Fitzmyer, Romans: A New Translation with Introduction and Commentary, Anchor Yale Bible 33 (New York: Doubleday, 1993).
source_note: PDFs not present in DOCTORAT folder; only .txt OCR extractions of the AYB 33 commentary are available. scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_free_will_an.locator: Rom 9:1–5, §31 'Paul's lament about his former coreligionists', COMMENT
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_free_will_an.chapter: Part C. This justification and salvation through faith do not contradict God's promises to Israel of old (9:1–11:36) — §31 (9:1–5)
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_free_will_an.quote_verbatim: Augustine, Aquinas, and Calvin have found in this passage one of the main supports of their doctrine of double predestination; Origen, Chrysostom, and Arminius have used it to confirm their belief that man's destiny rests on his own free response to God's grace; and the universalists have seized on it as one of the few Biblical texts which give grounds for belief in universal salvation. The irony is that all have been sound in their affirmations, though grievously at fault in their failure to appreciate the strength of the other two positions. For Paul actually contrives … to hold all three beliefs at the same time.
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_free_will_an.quote_note: Fitzmyer cites G. B. Caird, ExpTim 68 (1956–57): 324, approvingly in the COMMENT on Rom 9:1–5 to introduce the history-of-reception of predestination/free-will in chaps. 9–11.
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_free_will_an.context: Source line 34 of extraction. Fitzmyer endorses Caird's tripartite mapping (Augustinian double predestination / Origenist-Arminian free response / universalist), framing this as the interpretive grid for Rom 9–11. Confirms KG description that he presents the debate without himself adjudicating it.

scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_free_will_an.quote_verbatim: Augustine, Aquinas, and Calvin have found in this passage one of the main supports of their doctrine of double predestination; Origen, Chrysostom, and Arminius have used it to confirm their belief that man's destiny rests on his own free response to God's grace; and the universalists have seized on it as one of the few Biblical texts which give grounds for belief in universal salvation. … For Paul actually contrives … to hold all three beliefs at the same time.
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_free_will_an.context: Same Caird citation. Fitzmyer adopts the three-positions schema (double predestination / free response / universalism) and treats them as simultaneously held by Paul, not mutually exclusive — exactly the formulation captured in the KG argument description.

scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_divine_elect.locator: Rom 9:6–13, §32 'God's promises to Israel stem from his gratuitous election of it as his people; hence his word has not failed', COMMENT
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_divine_elect.quote_verbatim: From the examples used in this paragraph Paul seeks to show that the way God deals with contemporary Jews is the way he has dealt with the patriarchs of old. It may seem that God, in so dealing, is really unjust; but Paul will not tolerate that implication.
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_divine_elect.supporting_quote_2: 12. not because of deeds but because of his call. … The fundamental thesis of Romans is applied to Israel's patriarchal heritage. … All Paul says is that it was 'not because of deeds,' and says nothing about the basis on which the call was made, either God's foreknowledge, as John Chrysostom understood it (In ep. ad Romanos hom. 16.6 [PG 60.557]) or God's predestination, as Calvin did (Commentary on Romans [trans. J. Owen], 349).
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_divine_elect.context: Source lines 22 and 46 of extraction. The 'not because of deeds but because of his call' formula (Rom 9:11–12) is precisely the lemma cited in the KG description. Fitzmyer notes Paul refuses to draw the injustice consequence — but does not himself harmonize divine sovereignty and human agency, leaving the tension open (Chrysostom-foreknowledge vs. Calvin-predestination).

scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_the_scope_of.locator: Rom 9:6, §32 NOTES on 'not all descendants of Israel are truly Israel'
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_the_scope_of.quote_verbatim: It seems, rather, that 'Israel' in the second instance refers to Jewish Christians, to those of ethnic Israel who have put faith in Christ. Having made this distinction, Paul discusses ethnic Israel, seeking to refine its relation to God's election.
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_the_scope_of.context: Source line 34 of extraction (9.1-5 file, which actually covers through 9:13). Exactly matches the KG argument: 'Israel' (second occurrence in 9:6) = Jewish Christians, a subset of ethnic Israel defined by faith — not a broader Jew+Gentile community.

scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_freedom_and_.chapter: Romans 8 — Christian life empowered by the Spirit (8:1–13)
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_freedom_and_.quote_verbatim: Paul now introduces the counterpart of his discussion in chaps. 5–7. He has developed in a negative way the theme announced in 5:1–11, by explaining the freedoms that have come in Christ Jesus: freedom from sin and death (5:12–21); from sin and self (6:1–23); and from the law (7:1–25). Those who have put faith in Christ Jesus and have been baptized into his death, burial, and resurrection have become justified Christians, not only liberated from such evils, but also empowered to live a new life as the result of God's love manifested in the freeing acts of Christ Jesus.
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_freedom_and_.context: Source line 10 of Romans 8 extraction. Captures Fitzmyer's existential rather than metaphysical reading of Pauline freedom: liberation from enslavement (sin, death, self, law) and empowerment to a new mode of life by divine action, not Greek-style metaphysical libertarian free will.

scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_flesh_vs_spi.locator: Rom 8:5, NOTES on 'Those who live according to the flesh'
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_flesh_vs_spi.quote_verbatim: 5. Those who live according to the flesh are concerned about things of the flesh. … In v 4 Paul spoke of those 'who walk according to the flesh'; now he probes more deeply and speaks of hoi kata sarka ontes, lit., 'those who are according to the flesh,' those whose very being is dominated ontologically by sarx. He refers to unregenerate human beings, and their outlook is wholly that of sarx, so that they cannot help but do 'the deeds of the flesh' (see Gal 5:19).
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_flesh_vs_spi.supporting_quote_2: those who live according to the Spirit are concerned about things of the Spirit. I.e., those who are baptized, live 'in Christ Jesus' (8:1), and are open to the promptings of the Spirit. … Because Christ lives in Christians, they are no longer motivated by the things of the flesh. A thoroughgoing change has taken place in the Christian's whole existence because of faith and baptism.
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_flesh_vs_spi.context: Source lines 48–49 of Romans 8 extraction. Fitzmyer explicitly reads sarx and pneuma as two ontological modes of existence (unregenerate vs. baptized), with the transition effected by 'faith and baptism' / Christ's redemptive act — exactly the KG description.

scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_moral_respon.locator: Rom 8:13, NOTES on 'if through the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body'
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_moral_respon.quote_verbatim: if through the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. If the justified Christian responds to the promptings of the Spirit and cooperates with prevenient divine grace, even the 'deeds' of the 'body' will lead to eternal life. … Hence his implied exhortation: Make use of the Spirit received, and mortify the deeds of the body, for this is the debt owed to Christ Jesus who has graced you with his Spirit. … Paul is not speaking here only of ascetic practices … but of the inevitable consequence in Christian life of adaptation of oneself to the influence of the Spirit and divine grace.
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_moral_respon.context: Source line 72 of Romans 8 extraction. Direct support for KG claim: Christians cooperate with prevenient grace; agency is real ('put to death the deeds of the body') yet enabling power is entirely the Spirit. Cooperation, not passive determinism.

scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_predestinati.locator: Rom 8:28–30, §29 'The Christian called and destined for glory', COMMENT
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_predestinati.quote_verbatim: One encounters in these verses the first mention of 'predestination,' which Paul will again mention in chap. 9. The combination of the Pauline verses on this topic in these chapters led to a preoccupation with them in the predestinarian controversies of later centuries. What Paul asserts here in this regard is stated from a corporate point of view. He does not have in mind the predestination of individuals (either to glory or to damnation). Such an interpretation of these chapters began with Augustine in his controversy with Pelagians, and it has distracted interpreters of Romans from the main thrust of Paul's discussion in these chapters ever since.
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_predestinati.supporting_quote_2: Chapter 8 discusses many topics about the new life that Christians lead in the Spirit. … (f) 8:28–30: the destiny of the Christian called to glory; …
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_predestinati.context: Source lines 458 and 11 of Romans 8 extraction. Fitzmyer reads 8:28–30 as corporate destiny ('the Christian called to glory'), not individual predestinarian decree à la Augustine. Directly matches KG description.

scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_eschatologic.locator: Rom 5:1–11, COMMENT and NOTE on v 9
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_eschatologic.chapter: Romans 5 — 5:1–11 (Justified Christians experience peace, hope, reconciliation)
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_eschatologic.quote_verbatim: Having established the justification of human beings by grace and through faith in Christ Jesus, Paul begins to discuss the Christian experience in itself and explains how salvation is assured for the upright. Once justified, the Christian is reconciled to God and experiences a peace that distressing troubles cannot upset, a hope that knows no disappointment, and a confidence that salvation is assured.
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_eschatologic.supporting_quote_2: we shall all the more certainly be saved by him. A favor still greater than justification itself will be manifested to the Christian in the eschatological salvation that is to come. … justification is subordinated to salvation, and the latter is regarded as something begun but still to be consummated or brought to its full expression … yet that consummation is guaranteed.
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_eschatologic.context: Source lines 21 and 66 of Romans 5 extraction. Hope is grounded in the death and resurrection of Christ (cf. v 10 'reconciled … through the death of his Son … saved by his life'); present state of grace guarantees future salvation. Matches KG description.

scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_reconciliati.quote_verbatim: 6. While we were still helpless. Or 'weak.' So Paul describes the enduring condition of the unjustified person: incapable of doing anything to achieve rectitude in the sight of God. … In the face of such persistent weakness and helplessness stands God's action in Christ. … for the godless. So Paul describes the condition of the unjustified; because of sin they were asebeis, lit., 'without reverence (for God).'
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_reconciliati.supporting_quote_2: 10. For if, when we were God's enemies. … Sinners are not merely 'weak' or 'godless,' but have actually made themselves 'enemies' of God through their sin (8:7). … It aptly expresses the culmination of the human situation of opposition to God, which only God's initiative, based on his love, can remedy.
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_reconciliati.context: Source lines 52, 56 and 68 of Romans 5 extraction. Fitzmyer explicitly traces Paul's catalogue: helpless → godless → sinners → enemies, and concludes only divine initiative (love) can remedy — precise match for KG description.

scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_human_agency.quote_verbatim: now that we are justified through faith. Lit., 'justified from faith,' expressed by the aor. pass. ptc., which connotes the once-for-all action of Christ Jesus on behalf of humanity.
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_human_agency.supporting_quote_2: to this grace in which we now stand. Through Christ justified Christians enjoy the favor of God; they stand before his tribunal acquitted by the grace of Christ. … Their status of rectitude is not their own; it does not come from their merits, but from the grace of Christ.
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_human_agency.context: Source lines 32 and 40 of Romans 5 extraction. Fitzmyer's wording 'once-for-all action of Christ Jesus on behalf of humanity' and 'status of rectitude is not their own … but from the grace of Christ' is verbatim what the KG description paraphrases.

scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_identity_of_.locator: Rom 7:1–6, COMMENT 'One of the major problems in this chapter is, Of what law does Paul speak?'
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_identity_of_.quote_verbatim: None of the reasons provided in favor of 1 or 2 shows that Paul had a concept of law wider than that of the Mosaic law. Thomas Aquinas (In ep. ad Romanos 7.1 [Parma 13.66]) rejected the natural law explanation, recognizing that Paul, in speaking absolutely of 'the law,' elsewhere means the law of Moses. … Hence it seems better to understand nomos at least from v 1b on as referring to the Mosaic law, and the same seems to be intended in v 1a as well.
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_identity_of_.supporting_quote_2: I am speaking to those who know what law is. Lit., 'who know law,' nomos being anarthrous. Paul refers to the Mosaic law elsewhere without using the def. art. (2:12, 13, 14, 23, 25; 3:20, 21, 28, 31; 4:13; 5:13, 20; etc.), so the anarthrous use here may be explained in the same way.
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_identity_of_.context: Source lines 24–28 and 35 of Romans 7 extraction. Fitzmyer rejects the three rival readings of nomos in 7:1a (law-in-general / Roman law / Adamic commandment) and concludes Mosaic law throughout. The anarthrous-use argument is explicitly addressed — exactly the KG claim.

scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_law_sin_and_.locator: Rom 7:1, NOTE on 'the law has authority over a human being'
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_law_sin_and_.quote_verbatim: Paul uses of the law the vb. kyrieuein, which he also used in 6:9 and 14 of sin and death, thus drawing the law into the threesome that tyrannize human existence apart from Christ.
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_law_sin_and_.supporting_quote_2: from the law of sin and death. … one should not miss the collocation here of the three key words: law, sin, and death. They sum up the discussion of chaps. 5–7. The tyranny exercised by sin and ending in death is broken; the person who is in Christ is freed of them … (Rom 8:2 NOTE, Romans 8 extraction).
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_law_sin_and_.context: Source line 36 of Romans 7 extraction (verbatim 'threesome that tyrannize human existence apart from Christ') and line 335 of Romans 8 extraction confirm the collocation. Exact lexical match with KG description.

scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_paul_s_view_.quote_verbatim: law binds only the living (7:1, 4a); consequently, Christians who have died 'through the body of Christ' are no longer bound to observe the law. … Christians are like the Jewish wife whose husband has died. As she is freed from 'the law of the husband' through death, so Christians have died 'through the body of Christ' and they are freed from the law (7:2, 3, 4b).
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_paul_s_view_.supporting_quote_2: Paul does not say that the law itself dies or has died, nor does he say that for the Christian the law has been repealed or is nonexistent. The law is still in effect, indeed, but it is the Christian who has died to it.
scholarly_argument_fitzmyer_paul_s_view_.context: Source lines 22 and 36 of Romans 7 extraction. Direct support: freedom is not by abolition of law but by the believer's death-with-Christ; law remains in effect but loses dominion. Verbatim match for KG description.
